Anne is big (fact).  
From “big → blue” (rule G) we infer **Anne blue**.  
From “big → round” (rule H) we infer **Anne round**.  

Anne is big and round, so by “big ∧ round → nice” (rule C) we infer **Anne nice**.  

Anne is nice and blue, so by “nice ∧ blue → green” (rule D) we infer **Anne green**.  

Anne is green and blue, so by “green ∧ blue → young” (rule A) we infer **Anne young**.  

Anne is green and young, so by “green ∧ young → not furry” (rule E) we infer **Anne not furry**.  

Thus the statement “Anne is furry” is contradicted.

ANSWER: False

D. All nice, blue things are green. (If nice and blue then green.)
E. If something is green and young then it is not furry. (If green and young then not furry.)

We need to see if we can derive "Anne furry".

From fact 1: Anne big.

Rule G: big -> blue. So Anne blue.

Rule H: big -> round. So Anne round.

Now we have: Anne big, blue, round.

Rule C: big and round -> nice. So Anne nice.

Rule D: nice and blue -> green. We have Anne nice, blue. So Anne green.

Now we have Anne green.

Rule A: green and blue -> young. Anne green, blue => Anne young.

Now we have Anne young.

Rule B: furry and young -> nice. But we have nice; but this rule is forward: if furry & young then nice. We can't use it to infer furry from nice. So no.

Rule E: green and young -> not furry. We have green and young, so we can infer Anne not furry.

Thus we derived Anne not furry (contradiction with the statement we want to test). So statement "Anne furry" is contradicted by rule E: green and young -> not furry.

Thus "Anne furry" is false according to the knowledge base.
